sections.h2: Which office sends the Pensacola tax bill?
sections.html:
Escambia County's tax collector mails the bill for a Pensacola address, and the county's property appraiser supplies the value it is based on. Pensacola sits in Florida's panhandle, and one parcel inside the city limits answers to several taxing bodies at once.

The collector's own description lists the school board, the county commission, the City of Pensacola, the Town of Century, the Sheriff, the Downtown Improvement Board and the Northwest Florida Water Management District among the bodies it collects for. A downtown house may therefore carry a line that a house out in the county never sees. The collector's site has a search by name, address or account number, which shows the lines for your parcel.

The appraiser's FAQ is blunt about its limits: it has no jurisdiction over budgets, tax rates or special assessments. A complaint about a rate belongs with the taxing body that set it. A complaint about a value or an exemption belongs at escpa.org.

sections.h2: What is Pensacola like for a homeowner thinking of selling?
sections.html:
The city's own profile page, citing the Census Bureau, gives Pensacola 54,312 residents at the 2020 count, 22.67 square miles and household income at a median of $72,699 for 2019 to 2023. It also counts 5,334 veterans.

Spanish settlers under Don Tristan de Luna established the settlement in 1559, and the city calls itself America's First Settlement and the City of Five Flags. Naval Air Station Pensacola, the Blue Angels and Pensacola International Airport anchor local life, so military moves bring a steady flow of newcomers. Pensacola Beach lies on Santa Rosa Island, while Downtown Pensacola holds the historic district and Palafox Street.

The city profile also reports an average commute of 21.5 minutes, about 220 sunny days a year and a metro cost of living 5.80 percent under the national average, crediting FloridaWest. It counts more than 40 primary and secondary schools and says Pensacola International Airport serves over three million passengers a year. Those are points a buyer may weigh next to the tax bill.

Location inside the city can change the bill. The appraiser's millage page treats the Downtown Improvement Board as a separate authority and gives Pensacola Beach its own total. Pull the parcel record before you set an asking price, because a Beach address and a downtown address are not taxed alike.

sections.h2: What are the payment dates and discounts in Pensacola?
sections.html:
Bills go out in November. The tax collector's notice on Amendment 3 shows a 4 percent discount through December 2, 2026, then 3 percent for the rest of that month, 2 percent in January 2027 and 1 percent in February 2027. The full amount falls due in March 2027, and anything unpaid is delinquent on April 1, 2027.

That same notice reports that voters approved Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026. It says the vote leaves the 2026 bill alone and that new homestead exemption amounts begin with the 2027 tax year.

Escambia also offers a quarterly plan to taxpayers whose prior year taxes topped $100 and who have no mortgage escrow. Sign up by April 30 of the year you want to use it. The collector prints this schedule.

Quarterly plan terms printed by the Escambia County Tax Collector
InstallmentDueDiscount
FirstJune 306%
SecondSeptember 304.5%
ThirdDecember 313%
FourthMarch 31None

Miss the June payment and you drop out for that year, then receive an ordinary November bill. The first two payments are a quarter of last year's tax each, and the last two split what is actually owed. Separately, the collector may accept a partial payment toward current taxes, with no discount, if it comes with an application before April.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can a Pensacola homeowner claim?
sections.html:
Homestead comes first. The appraiser wants the application before March 1, and you qualify if you hold title, live in the home in good faith and make it your permanent home on January 1.

  • Homestead: $25,000 off every levy, plus up to $25,000 more on assessed value over $50,000 for levies other than school taxes.
  • Senior add-on: owners 65 by January 1 whose household adjusted gross income is under the yearly cap, printed as $38,686 for 2026. The county's $50,000 covers county taxes only, and a separate City of Pensacola $50,000 covers city taxes only.
  • Widow or widower: $5,000, supported by a death certificate.
  • Disability or blindness: $5,000, with proof from Social Security or a Florida physician.
  • Veterans: $5,000 for a disability rated at ten percent or higher, and homestead relief for a total, permanent service-connected disability.

The Save Our Homes limit holds yearly growth in a homestead's taxable value to the smaller of 3 percent or the Consumer Price Index change. The appraiser says the limit is lost on a sale, a rental or any change of ownership, and the next owner must apply fresh.

sections.h2: Who pays the Pensacola tax bill in the year of a sale?
sections.html:
Closing agents normally settle the current year, and the title company runs the numbers. Ask the agent for the parcel's payoff and confirm which years are paid, open or delinquent.

Ask how the current year gets divided with the buyer. If an earlier year was never paid, a tax certificate may already have been sold against the parcel, so get the exact balance from the collector's office before you sign. Owners who held the home as a homestead should also ask the appraiser about portability, which lets the Save Our Homes benefit follow you to a new Florida homestead if you set it up within the allowed window, up to $500,000 of benefit.

The buyer's first bill can look very different from yours. The sale resets the assessment to market value, so an asking price built around your old tax figure can mislead a buyer. Point them to the appraiser's record for the parcel.

  • Request a payoff figure from the collector.
  • Look up the deed history in the clerk's Official Records.
  • Tell the appraiser if you hold an exemption or classification that ends with the sale.

sections.h2: Where is a Pensacola deed recorded?
sections.html:
The Escambia clerk of court keeps the Official Records, with the search listed at escambiaclerk.com. Deed stamps run at seventy cents per $100 of price in every Florida county but Miami-Dade, and the Department of Revenue says the clerk takes the tax when a deed is recorded.

After recording, the appraiser updates the owner on the tax roll. A new name on the deed does not carry over your homestead, so a buyer who will live there has to apply on their own.

faqs.q: Does the city or the county send the Pensacola bill?
faqs.a: The county does. Escambia's tax collector issues it, and the City of Pensacola is one of several lines on it, next to the county, the school district and districts such as the Downtown Improvement Board.

faqs.q: When do Pensacola discounts begin and end?
faqs.a: They start with the November bill at 4 percent and step down monthly to 1 percent in February. For 2026 bills the collector prints 4 percent through December 2, 2026, with delinquency on April 1, 2027.

faqs.q: Can Pensacola owners split the bill into installments?
faqs.a: Yes, if last year's tax was over $100 and you have no escrow account. Apply by April 30; payments fall on June 30, September 30, December 31 and March 31.

faqs.q: What does the senior exemption give in Pensacola?
faqs.a: It gives $50,000 off county taxes and a separate $50,000 off city taxes for owners past 65 under the income cap. The appraiser prints the 2026 cap as $38,686, with applications closing March 1.

faqs.q: Will a Pensacola sale change the taxable value?
faqs.a: Yes. A sale counts as a change of ownership, so the parcel is reassessed at market value and the new owner must apply for their own homestead before the Save Our Homes limit starts again.
